summary_html: A **child is removed without exigency or warrant**, violating constitutional rights. Federal courts treat such removals as seizures under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, actionable via §1983.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — limits removals to lawful emergencies and requires judicial review  
- **U.S. Constitution (4th & 14th Amendments)** — protects family integrity; requires due process

primary_citations.citation_text: District of Columbia - D.C. Code § 4-1321.07 (Failure to make report)
District of Columbia - D.C. Code § 16-2304 (Right to counsel; party status)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
key_cases.holding: Individual District caseworkers had qualified immunity on the Fourth and Fifth Amendment claims because the contours of the exigency exception for warrantless child removals were not clearly established, but summary judgment for the District itself was vacated and remanded for Monell analysis of the removal policies.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling circuit authority on § 1983 wrongful-removal claims in the District, including qualified immunity and municipal liability.
key_cases.quote: the precise contours of when an exigency exists to justify removal without a warrant or pre-deprivation hearing are not settled

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: Probable cause supported the medical hold and shelter care of an infant with suspected shaken baby syndrome and the parents' Child Protection Register listing did not violate due process, but the warrantless seizure of the sibling from inside the family home was remanded for a determination whether exigent circumstances existed.
key_cases.relevance: It is the D.C. Court of Appeals' framework for a § 1983 claim that children were seized from the home without a warrant or exigency.
key_cases.quote: under the Fourth Amendment, a lawful seizure of children from their parents' custody requires a court order, e.g., a warrant, probable cause, or exigent circumstances

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: The warrantless entry into the apartment and seizure of an infant taken from a hospital nursery were justified by emergency circumstances, so the identification of the baby and the ensuing confession were not suppressed and the kidnapping conviction was affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: It states the rule a plaintiff invokes when a child is taken from inside the home without a warrant or true exigency.
key_cases.quote: Fourth Amendment law presumes that warrantless searches and seizures inside a home are unreasonable absent exigent circumstances

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: The District failed to carry its burden of showing that shelter care was necessary for a healthy five-month-old removed after her mother's hospitalization, even under the less demanding probable cause standard, so the shelter care order was reversed.
key_cases.relevance: It shows what an insufficiently supported removal looks like in the District's own appellate court.
key_cases.quote: Because we conclude that the District failed to carry its burden even under a less-demanding probable-cause standard, we assume without deciding that a probable-cause standard applies.

key_cases.case_name: Monell v. New York City Dept. of Social Servs.
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: Municipalities and other local government units are 'persons' subject to suit under § 1983, but only where execution of the government's own policy or custom inflicts the constitutional injury; there is no vicarious liability for wrongs committed solely by employees.
key_cases.relevance: It supplies the municipal-liability standard the District must be measured against on the remand ordered in Doe v. District of Columbia, which is the live theory once individual caseworkers obtain qualified immunity for a warrantless removal.
key_cases.quote: We conclude, therefore, that a local government may not be sued under § 1983 for an injury inflicted solely by its employees or agents.
